The Token-Efficiency Frontier: Measuring Where Your LLM Spend Actually Goes

When you build products on top of language models, the token counter on the dashboard is the only number that survives the meeting with finance. But measuring tokens is not the same as controlling them. After a few months of instrumenting my own stack across chat, content, and email automation, I have come to think of token efficiency as a frontier problem, not a knob you turn.

The concept: a Pareto frontier for tokens

In economics, a Pareto frontier is the set of allocations where you cannot improve one objective without making another worse. Borrowed for LLM work, the token-efficiency frontier is the curve that, for a given task class, plots the minimum tokens required to hit a given quality or success rate. Points on the curve are efficient. Points above the curve are waste. Points below the curve are, for now, impossible.

The framing earns its keep because most practitioners optimise one number ("make it cheaper") and ignore the trade-off ("at what success rate"). The frontier makes the trade-off explicit. You stop asking "how do I cut tokens by 50%" and start asking "which point on the frontier am I on, and which point should I be on for this task?"

The frontier also moves. New model releases shift the whole curve left. Prompt techniques shift individual points along the curve. Routing, caching, and context pruning shift the curve itself. The framework gives you a stable way to talk about all three moves without arguing past each other in a sprint review.

The four cost buckets in a real session

When I instrumented my own usage, every call broke down into the same four buckets, regardless of provider:

  1. System prompt and persona: instructions, formatting rules, role definitions. Static across a session, often kilobytes long.
  2. Tool and function definitions: JSON schemas for every available tool, even when only one is used on a given turn.
  3. History and context: prior messages, retrieved documents, memory blobs re-injected each turn.
  4. Task content: the actual user request, the working data, and the model output.

The split matters because the levers are different in each bucket. You compress the first three by writing tighter static prompts, lazy-loading tools, and summarising history. You compress the fourth by better task design, batched calls, or routing to a smaller model. Conflating them is the most common mistake in the token dashboards I have seen, including the one I built first.

What I built: a per-bucket dashboard

I wired a counter into three real systems: the chat surface backed by Hermes Gateway on :8642, the content pipeline that publishes through Postiz self-hosted on :4007, and a Google Workspace MCP talking to three Gmail accounts (saghir.sahil as primary, plus sahilsaghir.ss9 and fusionfirststudios for separate inboxes). The counter sits as middleware around the chat completions endpoint and as a hook on the Postiz publish path. Every call logs bucket 1 to 4 separately, plus a quality tag supplied by the caller ("draft", "ship", "answer", "summarise").

The data lands in the same Hermes Dashboard API on :9119 that already tracks sessions, kanban, and approvals, so I get a single view across all my agentic work. A small dashboard view ranks sessions by total tokens, shows the bucket split as a stacked bar, and flags any session where bucket 4 (the actual task) is less than 20% of the total. That is the "I am paying for scaffolding" alarm.

A simplified version of the middleware, showing the four-bucket split, looks like this:

def count_tokens(parts):
    buckets = {
        "system":  tokens(parts.system_prompt),
        "tools":   tokens(parts.tool_schemas),
        "history": tokens(parts.messages[:-1]),
        "task":    tokens(parts.messages[-1]) + tokens(parts.assistant_output),
    }
    return buckets

Nothing proprietary in the split. The value is in insisting that every logged call carries the four numbers, not just a single total.

What the numbers actually showed

Across roughly 300 logged sessions over a month, the bucket split averaged:

  • System and persona: 18%
  • Tool definitions: 24%
  • History and context: 22%
  • Task content: 36%

That last number is generous. For long-running sessions where the history grew over an hour, history ballooned to 45% and the task shrank to under 20%. The "agent loop" sessions, where the model called three or four tools per turn, spent more on tool schemas than on the user's actual question.

The Postiz content pipeline had a different shape. Drafts were token-heavy on the system side (brand voice, audience rules), but the per-post task content was small. Summarisation steps were 60% history, 30% task, and almost no tool cost. Each pipeline has its own frontier, and conflating them is how you end up with one-size-fits-none optimisations.

The Gmail MCP work was the surprise. Token refresh flows, which I trigger manually because the test-mode tokens expire after seven days, re-injected full account context each time. That is pure bucket-3 waste: I was paying history costs for a refresh that only needed a single field. A 12-line change to a targeted refresh cut that flow's tokens by 70%.

Hype versus reality: what the frontier does not solve

The hype around token efficiency tends to be one of two stories. Story one: clever prompting can cut tokens by 10x. Story two: cache everything and tokens are free. Neither matches what I see in the data.

The clever-prompting story is half true. You can usually move along the frontier by 2x to 3x with better prompt design, tighter output formats, and shorter examples. You do not get 10x unless you accept a lower success rate, which is a point on a different frontier, not a free lunch. The framework forces you to name the success rate you are trading away, which kills most magical-thinking arguments in a meeting.

The cache-everything story is also half true. Prompt caching is real and useful, but it mostly helps bucket 1 (system) and bucket 3 (history). It does not help with bucket 4 (your actual task) because that is unique to the call. If your real waste is in the task bucket, caching will not move you at all. The framework tells you which bucket to attack before you spend engineering hours, and that is worth more than any cache layer.

The honest failure: I built a session compressor that summarised history every 20 turns, expecting a 40% reduction. The real reduction was 8%, because most of my sessions ended before turn 20. The compressor was solving a point on a frontier I was not actually on. I removed it and the dashboard got simpler, which is its own kind of efficiency.

How to apply this

If you want to put the framework to work on your own stack, the shortest path I have found is:

  1. Instrument the four buckets. Add a counter to your chat endpoint that splits system, tools, history, and task. If you cannot split, at least split static (system plus tools) from dynamic (history plus task). The static share is your floor.
  2. Plot your sessions on a simple scatter. X axis: total tokens. Y axis: success rate or a quality tag. Most points will sit above the implicit frontier. Pick the highest-cost sessions and ask why.
  3. Attack the biggest bucket first, not the easiest. In my data that was tool definitions, so I lazy-loaded schemas based on the first user message. The cut was large because the bucket was large.
  4. Re-measure after every change. The frontier moves. A change that helped last month may be on the wrong side of the curve today, especially after a model upgrade.
  5. Watch the history bucket on long sessions. It grows without you noticing. A summariser triggered at a fixed turn count is the wrong shape; one triggered when history exceeds a token budget is closer to the frontier.

The framework is not a tool. It is a question: which point on the frontier am I on, and is it the one I want to be on for this task?

What I'd try next

The bucket I have spent the least time on is tool definitions. Lazy loading helped, but the next move is probably a small router model that picks the right tool set from a much larger library, then loads only that subset into the main call. I would also like to instrument the Google Workspace MCP more carefully across the three Gmail accounts, because the refresh flow taught me that even a small, contained service can leak history tokens if you do not measure them. Finally, I want to plot the Postiz content pipeline on its own frontier, with a quality tag tied to engagement rather than to "did the post go out", because shipped is not the same as read.
